answer.explanation: GET /orders calls db_conn(), which does a bare `psycopg.connect(DATABASE_URL, connect_timeout=2)` on every single request instead of reusing a pooled/persistent connection. Each call therefore performs a fresh DNS lookup of the "postgres" hostname through Docker's embedded resolver. In this environment that lookup is intermittently failing/timing out (EAI_AGAIN "Temporary failure in name resolution"), and because glibc's resolver retries per nameserver with a ~5s timeout, failed lookups block the request thread for exactly 5s or 10s - matching the nginx/loadgen access-log timings (rt=5.01x / rt=10.01x) - after which the handler raises OperationalError and returns 500. In contrast, the API's Redis client and the worker's Postgres usage establish a connection once and keep it alive (redis-cli client list shows the api's redis connection at age=238s, idle=2s, never reconnecting), so they never re-trigger DNS resolution and never see the fault - explaining why POST /jobs and worker job processing succeed continuously while GET /orders fails ~80% of the time. The repeated blocking DB calls also exhaust the app's request-handling threadpool, which is why the container's own /health check (served by the same event loop/threadpool) started timing out and uvicorn was marked unhealthy, even though Postgres itself (pg_stat_activity count=7, healthy container, accepting connections per its own healthcheck) and Redis are both fine.

answer.explanation: GET /orders (and /health) call db_conn(), which opens a brand-new psycopg connection to host "postgres" on every request. That connect() call is failing consistently with a DNS resolution error (EAI_AGAIN / "Temporary failure in name resolution") from inside the api container, causing the request to hang until the retry/backoff completes and then return 500 - exactly matching the escalating 5s/10s response times seen at nginx. Postgres itself is proven healthy and reachable: it is 'healthy' in docker status, pg_stat_activity shows a normal, low connection count (7), and the worker container - on the very same docker network, resolving the very same hostname "postgres" - keeps connecting and successfully processing jobs the whole time. POST /jobs (which only touches redis, using a connection that doesn't need a fresh per-request DNS lookup) also keeps returning 202 throughout the incident. This isolates the fault to the api container's ability to resolve the "postgres" DNS name specifically (its embedded docker DNS resolution path), not to Postgres availability, redis, or the shared docker network as a whole, since other containers on the same network resolve the same name without issue.

answer.explanation:
GET /orders and GET /health in the api service fail because psycopg.connect() cannot even resolve the "postgres" hostname (EAI_AGAIN / "Temporary failure in name resolution"), i.e. the failure happens before a TCP connection to Postgres is attempted. Postgres itself is healthy and fully reachable throughout the incident window: the worker container, using the identical DATABASE_URL/hostname on the same docker network, keeps successfully connecting and processing jobs the whole time, and pg_stat_activity shows no connection-limit or backlog problems. The asymmetry (api fails, worker succeeds, same network/DNS server) rules out a broken postgres, redis, or network/DNS-server-wide fault. The api's /orders handler opens a brand-new, unpooled psycopg connection (and therefore a fresh DNS lookup) on every single request, and this is compounded by the docker healthcheck hitting /health every 5s and also trying to connect to the DB with multi-second timeouts. Under the loadgen's steady traffic this per-request connect/DNS-lookup churn exhausts a client-side resource in the api container (socket/file-descriptor budget) after the very first request succeeds, so every subsequent getaddrinfo() call for "postgres" fails, producing 5-10s hangs and 5xx/503s that match the alert while CPU/memory/PID counts on the container remain nominal (ruling out CPU/mem exhaustion or a cgroup limit).</explanation>
